chunks.text: Amla (Phyllanthus emblica), also called emblic or Indian gooseberry, is a deciduous tree in the family Phyllanthaceae native to tropical and southern Asia and widely cultivated across India. It is a relatively small tree, growing 1-8 metres tall, with mottled bark and flowers appearing mainly in March-April; grafted trees begin flowering within 3-4 years, versus 7-10 years for trees grown from seed. The fruit is nearly spherical, light greenish-yellow, smooth and hard, with six faint vertical furrows; wild fruit weighs only around 5.5 grams, while cultivated varieties can weigh 28-56 grams. The fruit's sharp sourness and bitterness come from a very high concentration of tannins such as emblicanin A and B, punigluconin and pedunculagin, along with flavonoids and ellagic acid, and it is known for an exceptionally high vitamin C content.

chunks.text: Amla fruit is eaten raw or cooked, and across South Asia it is traditionally pickled with salt, oil and spices, added to dal, or made into a sugar-candied preserve called amle ka murabbah; in Indonesia, Batak communities use the inner bark in a traditional fish soup. Dried and fresh amla fruit is a staple ingredient in Ayurvedic medicine. The fruit carries religious significance in Hinduism, where it is associated with the Trimurti, and in Buddhist tradition it is said that Emperor Ashoka, on his deathbed, gave away half an emblic fruit as his final act of charity to the Buddhist sangha; the Hindu festival Amalaka Ekadashi is dedicated to worship of the amla tree in honour of Vishnu.
